question: Tell me about a time independent thinking was unwelcome. What did you do anyway?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project, the team lead wanted to hardcode a config value because it was faster to ship. I thought it would break future deploys so I wrote a short doc showing the two-line change and what it would cost us in six months.
What happened when you shared it?
He still said no, so I asked if I could add it as a comment in the code for the next person. He agreed. Later the same config caused an incident and the comment helped us fix it in ten minutes.
How did you feel about the initial pushback?
It was uncomfortable but I realized I needed to show the concrete risk instead of just saying it was bad practice.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time independent thinking was unwelcome. What did you do anyway?
Role: new grad on first project, lead wanted to hardcode config
Action: wrote one-page doc with future cost, then asked for a comment when doc was rejected
Outcome: comment saved 10 min on later incident
Quote: "I realized I needed to show the concrete risk instead of just saying it was bad practice"
Follow-up: How did you feel about the initial pushback? → focused on showing data next time
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Challenge skillfully at junior level. Candidate described a small-scope situation where the lead rejected their input yet still found a low-friction way to protect the code. The concrete quote about learning to show risk rather than opinion shows coachability. The outcome (comment used in incident) is local but measurable. Biggest strength is that they adapted their approach after the first no instead of escalating or dropping it.

lowerTranscript.text: My manager told me to just copy the old design even though I knew it had a bug. I mentioned it once in standup and he said we don't have time so I dropped it.
Did you do anything after that?
No, I just did what he asked. I figured he had more context.

junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Challenge skillfully at junior level. The candidate stopped after one mention and explicitly deferred to authority without trying any other approach. The story shows no ownership of the known bug and no attempt to document the risk even for their own learning. Biggest gap is absence of any follow-up action once resistance appeared.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were about to duplicate a payments service because leadership wanted both to hit their quarterly OKRs. I pulled the data on overlap and shared a one-pager with both leads showing 40% shared code paths.
One lead still pushed to build separately. I asked if we could run a two-week spike together instead of committing to full builds. We did the spike and ended up sharing the service.
I showed the maintenance cost would hit both teams in the next year and that the spike let us keep both OKRs while reducing long-term load.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time independent thinking was unwelcome. What did you do anyway?
Situation: two teams duplicating payments work for OKRs
Action: data one-pager then proposed joint spike after initial rejection
Outcome: shared service instead of duplicate
Quote: "I showed the maintenance cost would hit both teams in the next year"
Follow-up: What trade-off did you surface? → maintenance cost and OKR compatibility
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Challenge skillfully at senior level. Candidate used data and a low-cost experiment to change direction across two teams without authority. The spike proposal after the first rejection shows influence without forcing a binary fight. Concrete metric (40% shared paths) and the maintenance-cost framing demonstrate strategic judgment. Biggest strength is turning resistance into a joint experiment that preserved both teams' goals.

lowerTranscript.text: Leadership wanted to split a shared library into two copies so each team could move faster. I sent an email with my concerns and never heard back so I moved on.
Did you follow up with anyone?
I mentioned it in one 1:1 with my manager but he said the decision was already made.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time independent thinking was unwelcome. What did you do anyway?

Outcome: accepted the decision after no reply
Quote: "I mentioned it in one 1:1 with my manager but he said the decision was already made"
Follow-up: Did you follow up with anyone? → only the single 1:1
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Challenge skillfully at senior level. The candidate relied on a single email and one manager conversation without attempting cross-team influence or proposing an alternative path. No metrics or trade-offs were surfaced to the actual decision makers. Biggest gap is lack of persistence or creative workaround once the first channel was closed.

raiseTranscript.text: The board wanted to acquire a company whose product overlapped 70% with our roadmap. I built a short model showing the integration cost would erase the revenue synergy in year two.
How did you surface this given the momentum?

I asked the CEO for a private 30-minute walk-through before the next board meeting and framed it as a diligence gap rather than opposition. We ended up renegotiating the deal terms instead of walking away.
The board now requires a 2-page integration-risk memo on any acquisition above $50M.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time independent thinking was unwelcome. What did you do anyway?

Outcome: renegotiated terms and new board process for future deals

exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Challenge skillfully at exec level. Candidate changed a board-level acquisition path by using a private channel and neutral framing instead of public opposition. The creation of an ongoing process (integration-risk memo) shows organizational leverage beyond the single decision. The story balances short-term deal protection with long-term governance improvement. Biggest strength is strategic judgment in choosing the right audience and framing to make independent analysis land.

lowerTranscript.text: The CEO announced a re-org that removed two layers of review I thought were necessary for risk. I raised it in the exec meeting and was told the decision was final so I focused on executing the new structure.
I documented my concerns in an email to the CEO after the meeting but did not pursue further.
